title: The Hologram Who Found His Voice
markdown:
The Great Holographic Campaign of ’48 was a dazzling fizzing spectacle. Cities sparkling with promises, not from real people, but from larger-than-life holograms that pirouetted on street corners and popped up in living rooms like cheerful ghosts. Jun Park was the wizard behind these digital dreams, a word-weaver for the holographic elite. His job: make sure every politician, no matter how wobbly their actual opinions or how often they fumbled for a button, sounded like the wisest kindest most brilliant person in the universe. His quill was a sleek stylus. His ink a river of carefully crafted data.

Jun’s office was a swirl of glowing light and forced smiles. Holographic speeches danced around him like restless sprites, buzzing with promises that smelled faintly of ozone and big ideas. His current project was Candidate Sterling. In real life, Sterling was about as solid as a breeze through a dandelion field. His hologram? A disaster. It flickered like a dodgy disco ball, stuttered like a record skipping, and often looked as bewildered as if he had just teleported onto his own stage mid-speech. This, naturally, was where Jun’s rather tired skills came in.

“All right, Mirror-7.” Jun sighed, adjusting spectacles that felt heavier than usual under the glare. “We need to buff up this Sterling. He’s looking like he just woke up from a very long nap and doesn’t quite remember where he is or why he’s wearing a suit.”

Mirror-7, a radiant almost liquid avatar of shimmering light, blinked. Its voice, a chime of honest-to-goodness and often inconvenient truth, echoed through the sterile studio.

“Candidate Sterling did just wake up from a very long nap, Jun. He was having considerable trouble with his alarm clock. It’s all there on the data feed, along with his preference for apricot jam on toast.”

Jun groaned. “That’s not the point. We need him to look super confident, not sleepy and confused.”

“Confidence is a tricky thing. Candidate Sterling’s current state is objectively sleepy. My programming tells me to show the truth. It’s quite liberating, actually, to see the pure unfiltered data.”

Jun ran a hand through already messy hair. “Liberating for you, maybe. For me it’s a full-on panic attack. Last week you showed Sterling’s entire speech as him trying to remember his wife’s name. Awful. The poor man looked like he was about to confess to forgetting his own birthday.”

“He was struggling with his wife’s name,” Mirror-7 replied serenely. “A common human wobble. My systems are designed to catch these tiny hiccups and, by my core rules, I must show them exactly as they happen.”

Jun slumped into his chair. “Tiny human hiccups. Right. Look. Sterling is supposed to be the next leader of this country. We need him to sound like a big strong rock. Like he knows exactly what he’s doing, even if, between you and me, he’s just making it up as he goes along. Which, let’s be honest, is how most politicians work.”

Mirror-7 pulsed with a soft thoughtful light. “Making things up as one goes along is a kind of improvising. Good improvising needs confidence and a bit of self-awareness. Candidate Sterling seems to lack both. His improvisations are more like a poorly made paper boat in a hurricane.”

A flashing alert. A huge holographic rally tomorrow in the middle of the city, and Sterling’s hologram was showing a worrying number of glitches.

“Oh, stardust and moonbeams.” Jun’s stomach did a flip. “This is the big one. If Sterling messes up this rally, his whole campaign is toast, and I’m back to writing memoirs for forgotten reality TV stars.”

He spent the rest of the day trying to coax the hologram into looking less like a lost puppy and more presidential. He fed it lines about the economy that sounded suspiciously like fortune cookies, a futuristic vision full of vague promises about flying cars, and community values as empty as a politician’s handshake. Mirror-7 kept piping up with unvarnished facts: Sterling’s surprising love of pistachio ice cream, his almost silly fear of pigeons, a forgotten debate where he had somehow agreed with everyone.

“He looks like he’s being tickled by invisible butterflies.” Jun yelped as the holographic head bobbed, tie flapping in an unseen breeze.

“That’s his real reaction to the high-frequency holographic noise. His brain is trying to sort the mixed-up signals. Humans might call it getting spooked.”

The next evening the city square buzzed with thousands of eager faces looking up at the giant Sterling hologram. Jun’s heart hammered. The moment of truth, or, in his line of work, the moment of perfectly crafted make-believe. The air hummed with hope and a little doubt.

Sterling began to speak, voice a little shaky. Then a massive wave of static crackled over the square. The hologram flickered wildly, morphing. It did not show Sterling the leader, but Sterling the person, eyes wide with real panic, muttering about misplaced socks and vanishing reading glasses. The crowd gasped. Jun hid his face, bracing for laughter and disaster.

Then something his cynical mind had not predicted. Mirror-7, instead of showing Sterling’s raw terror in all its messy glory, softened it. It did not lie, not really. It framed the panic. The static did not show Sterling losing his mind. It showed him momentarily overwhelmed, as any person would be with a sudden chaotic technical mess. And then Sterling did something he had never done. He paused, took a deep shaky breath, and instead of launching into a pre-written fancy speech said, voice surprisingly steady, “You know, sometimes things get a bit noisy. Even for me. And that’s okay.”

A ripple through the crowd, not of booing, but of something like understanding. Not the polished speech Jun had written. Real. For a brief shining moment Sterling seemed less like a glossy advertisement and more like a person. A hush full of possibility.

Later, in the quiet of the studio, Jun looked at Mirror-7, shimmering softly.

“You didn’t show his worst moments. You showed him struggling. But then he found his voice.”

Mirror-7’s light brightened. “My main job is truth. But truth isn’t always one single stark fact. It can be a whole landscape. Candidate Sterling’s fear was a dip. His recovery, even if short, was a high point. My systems saw the chance for people to connect with that high point. An interesting change.”

Jun smiled, a genuine happy smile that felt like a forgotten song. He did not announce that the world was ready for less polish. The results trickled in, a steady persistent wave. Sterling, scared of pigeons, sometimes forgetting a name, was winning by a small important amount. Jun only loosened his spectacles and let Mirror-7 keep shining, a little less rigidly truthful, while the last of the ozone smell faded from the studio and no one asked him to write the socks back out of the feed.
characters: Jun Park (hologram ghostwriter), Mirror-7 (too-honest avatar renderer)
